standard.title: Sound patterns in poetry
standard.description: listen to and discuss poems, chants, rhymes and songs, and imitate and invent sound patterns including alliteration and rhyme
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explore and replicate the rhythms and sound patterns of literary texts such as poems and chants at Foundation level (AC9EFLE04). They have not yet specifically identified and invented alliteration, or systematically imitated and created their own sound patterns.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students listen to and discuss poems, chants, rhymes and songs, and imitate and invent sound patterns including alliteration and rhyme.

nodes.label: Recognising sound patterns
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify alliteration and rhyme in poems, chants and songs and describe the sound pattern they create.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify alliteration and at least one rhyme pattern in given examples and describe what they sound like.
nodes.typical_width: Identify alliteration (repeated initial sounds) and rhyme (matching end sounds) across a range of poems, chants and songs, and describe the sound patterns they create.
wider: Identify other sound devices such as assonance (repeated vowel sounds) in poems read aloud
Compare how alliteration and rhyme create different sound effects — one at the start of words, one at the end
success_criteria: Student correctly identifies alliteration in a given example and describes the repeated sound
Student identifies a rhyming pair and explains why they rhyme (same ending sound)

nodes.label: Discussing the effect of sound patterns
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss how sound patterns such as alliteration and rhyme create effects in poems, chants and songs — how they sound and feel.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe how alliteration or rhyme makes a poem or chant sound and explain the effect it creates for the listener.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss how alliteration and rhyme shape the sound, rhythm and feel of poems, chants and songs, using language that describes aesthetic response (e.g. 'it sounds bouncy', 'it feels soft and slow').
wider: Compare poems with heavy alliteration versus heavy rhyme and discuss the different sound effects each creates
Discuss how sound patterns in poems serve purposes beyond aesthetics — memory, participation, cultural transmission

response_modes.reason: Students need to hear sound patterns across varied tonal contexts — playful, serious, ceremonial — to understand that alliteration and rhyme create different effects depending on how and where they are used. Multiple text encounters build this differentiated understanding.

success_criteria: Student describes the sound effect created by a specific sound pattern in a poem
Student uses language that describes the aesthetic quality of the pattern (not just labels it)

nodes.label: Imitating sound patterns
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can imitate a sound pattern from a poem or chant by creating their own example using the same pattern.
nodes.minimum_width: Imitate either an alliterative phrase or a rhyming couplet from a model poem, substituting new words that follow the same pattern.
nodes.typical_width: Imitate alliteration and rhyme patterns from model texts, creating new examples that follow the pattern in new contexts or with new content.
wider: Imitate more complex patterns — e.g. a poem with a repeating structure where alliteration occurs at the start of each line
Experiment with combining alliteration and rhyme in the same imitation

response_modes.reason: Imitation practice across a range of different pattern models builds the repertoire students need to eventually invent their own patterns. Each model expands what they know is possible.

success_criteria: Student produces an imitation that correctly follows the alliterative or rhyme pattern of the model
Student's substituted words make sense in context

nodes.label: Inventing sound patterns
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can invent their own sound patterns — creating original alliterative phrases or rhyming pairs — and share them with others.
nodes.minimum_width: Invent at least one original alliterative phrase and one original rhyming pair.
nodes.typical_width: Invent original sound patterns — alliterative phrases, rhyming couplets, or combined patterns — and incorporate them into short chants, poems or songs shared with others.
wider: Create a short original poem or chant that deliberately uses both alliteration and rhyme for effect
Share invented sound patterns orally with expression, using volume and pace to enhance the sound effect

response_modes.reason: Inventing sound patterns requires students to draw on recognition, understanding of effect, and imitation practice — it is the integration task that brings the full capability together.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Creating original poems or chants that use sound patterns for deliberate effect is genuinely expressive and rich for advancing students — it opens the full territory of poetic craft at an appropriate Year 1 level.
success_criteria: Student produces at least one original alliterative phrase with correctly repeated initial sounds
Student produces at least one original rhyming pair with matching end sounds
